title: Check the urgency
body: Some deadlines are real, and some demands only feel immediate. Pause long enough to check the facts, the actual deadline, and what needs attention first.

title: Choose where attention goes
body: Attention is limited. You can make a task easier by reducing competition for it and deciding what deserves your next few minutes.

title: Practise a manageable challenge
body: A useful challenge is small, chosen, and suitable for your circumstances. Build confidence through practice rather than forcing yourself through distress.

title: Notice a thought without obeying it
body: A thought can be useful information, a prediction, or an old habit. Notice it, look at what supports it, and decide how you want to respond.

title: Pause before joining the outrage
body: A strong reaction can signal something you care about. Before sharing or replying, check the source and choose an action that serves the issue.

title: Make the helpful choice easier
body: The environment influences habits. Add a small obstacle to an unhelpful routine and remove one obstacle from the action you want to take.

title: Use precise words instead of fixed labels
body: Labels can hide details. Describe the behaviour, situation, or need clearly enough that you can respond to what is actually happening.

title: Make room for quiet
body: Quiet can offer a break from stimulation. It does not have to stop your thoughts; let it be a chance to notice your surroundings without adding another input.

title: Let approval be information
body: Feedback can help, but it cannot define your whole worth. Separate useful guidance from the pressure to please everyone.

title: Begin before everything feels ready
body: You may not need complete confidence to take a small step. Choose an action that is safe and manageable, and let the result guide your next step.

title: Reduce the open loops
body: Unfinished tasks can occupy attention. Put them in one trusted place, choose a next step, and remember that tiredness can also call for ordinary rest or care.

title: Question the message behind the comparison
body: Some messages encourage dissatisfaction to sell a solution. Ask what is being offered, what evidence supports it, and whether it meets a need you actually have.

title: State a clear boundary
body: A boundary describes what you can offer or accept. Keep it clear, consider your circumstances, and choose a safe way to communicate it.

title: Name the feeling and the next decision
body: Thinking can help solve a problem, but repeated analysis sometimes goes nowhere. Name what you feel, then decide whether you need information, action, support, or a pause.

title: Find the simplest useful next step
body: Some problems are complex. A practical response can still begin with one clear step, while leaving room for more information or help.

title: Listen to body cues with curiosity
body: Physical sensations can have many causes. Notice them without immediately deciding what they mean, and meet an ordinary need or seek appropriate help when needed.

title: Work with the part you can influence
body: Your effort matters, while outcomes also depend on other people and circumstances. Choose a useful input and decide when to review the result.

title: Choose some time without an audience
body: A little time alone can help you notice your own preferences. Balance it with connection and adapt it to what feels helpful for you.

title: Compare with more context
body: What you see of someone else is incomplete. Use a comparison only if it offers information you can use in your own circumstances.

title: Return to what is happening now
body: The past can teach and the future can guide planning. When thought becomes repetitive, return to the next action available in the present.

title: Choose within real circumstances
body: You cannot control every system or circumstance. You can notice where a choice exists, seek support, and take a step that reflects what matters to you.
